subject_line: The house that gives Shirley its name
email_body:
Dear Ronnie,

Shirley caught my attention for its timing: Melbourne in the narrow weeks between the end of the Black Summer fires and the start of the pandemic, seen by a Collingwood narrator whose food-celebrity mother has left her behind after the trouble over the family house. I'd love to ask why you chose that in-between stretch of time, and how you decided which corners of the inner north would carry the story.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. The portrait is developed through a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: Shirley (Hamish Hamilton 2023) set in Melbourne between Black Summer and the pandemic, Collingwood narrator, mother a food celebrity, title from the family house (Readings/SRB reviews); shortlisted Christina Stead Prize & Voss Prize (RMIT). book_title: Crime Fiction from a Professional Eye: Women Writers with Law Enforcement and Justice Experience
subject_line: Women who wrote crime after working it
email_body:
Dear Lili,

I came across Crime Fiction from a Professional Eye and was struck by its premise: reading crime novels by women who had worked as lawyers, forensic experts or detectives before writing them. I'd be curious to hear what first drew you to that overlap between professional experience and fiction, and whether co-editing True Crime and Women changed how you think about it.

subject_line: Following Ernst Dieffenbach from Giessen to New Zealand
email_body:
Dear Thom,

The Naturalist follows Ernst Dieffenbach from radical politics in Giessen, through prison and exile in London, to his voyage out with the New Zealand Company as one of the first scientists to work in New Zealand. I'd like to ask how you balanced the documented record of his life against the parts you had to imagine, and how that first novel shaped what came after, from The Salted Air to editing Headland.

subject_line: Kate, Vee and the idea of a replacement
email_body:
Dear Liz,

Catherine Wheel caught my eye for Kate's fixation on Vee, the woman she sees as her 'replacement', and for its origins as your PhD novel at the University of Tasmania. With your background in journalism and psychotherapy, I'd love to ask how much that clinical experience shaped the way you built Kate's obsession, and how it is feeding into the second novel about women in the rock industry.

book_title: The Alphabet of Light and Dark
subject_line: Three names: Danielle Wood, Minnie Darke and Angelica Banks
email_body:
Dear Danielle,

I've been reading about the different names you write under: The Alphabet of Light and Dark and Mothers Grimm as Danielle Wood, Star-crossed as Minnie Darke, and the Tuesday McGillycuddy books as Angelica Banks with Heather Rose. I'd be curious to ask how each name changes the way you approach a book, and whether teaching in Hobart pulls you towards one more than the others.

email_body:

I'd love to ask what it was like to go back to that material years later, writing for a different readership, and how leading the creative writing program at the University of Tasmania shapes your own writing life.
